#### Sentinel-3C returns its first thermal-infrared Earth images

ESA reported on **18 November 2026** that the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer aboard **Copernicus Sentinel-3C** has produced its first thermal-infrared and shortwave-infrared images. The satellite launched on **15 September**; the displayed scenes were acquired over southwestern Europe and North Africa on **2 November** and Western Australia on **4 November**. SLSTR has nine visible, shortwave-infrared and thermal-infrared bands, including two channels intended for detecting and monitoring wildfire intensity. [ESA commissioning report](https://www.esa.int/articles/about-us/directorates/earth-observation-programmes/copernicus/sentinel-3/first-thermal-images-from-sentinel-3c-radiometer).

The Western Australia scene resolves top-of-atmosphere brightness temperatures above 40 °C over parts of the land, around 20 °C over the eastern Indian Ocean, vegetation structure and recent burn scars. Brightness temperature is not identical to physical surface temperature, and the instrument was still being commissioned. These are engineering and calibration images demonstrating that the channels operate, not a new climate trend measurement; validated continuity with Sentinel-3A/3B records still requires full calibration.

#### Device-independent quantum position verification beats equal-latency classical localization

Gautam Kavuri and colleagues report in a **peer-reviewed Nature article published 18 November** a remote position-verification experiment whose security depends on observed Bell correlations and relativistic timing rather than trusted quantum hardware. A loophole-free Bell test across a quantum network was used against adversaries that could be weakly entangled before each trial. The demonstrated one-dimensional localization interval was **2.47(2) times smaller** than the best necessarily non-remote classical protocol; against classical protocols with identical latency, the localization volume was **4.53(5) times smaller**. [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11247-3).

The experiment establishes a certifiable quantum advantage for its threat model and network geometry. It is not yet a field-ready geolocation service: the demonstrated protocol treats a restricted experimental adversary, while general security depends on stated assumptions about entanglement resources, timing, loss and station separation. Deployment would also need authenticated infrastructure and robust long-distance quantum links.

#### A two-dimensional Bose gas simulates a massive relativistic quantum field

Yansheng Zhang and colleagues report in an **open-access, peer-reviewed Nature article published 18 November** an analogue simulation of a massive relativistic field in **2+1 dimensions**. Two coherently coupled spin components in a uniform two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate encode the long-wavelength sine-Gordon field in their relative phase. In the perturbative regime the excitations show relativistic dispersion with a tunable mass gap; outside that regime the experiment directly observes topological domain walls across which the phase winds by **2π**. [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11268-y).

The platform makes real-time, non-perturbative dynamics experimentally accessible in more than one spatial dimension and could emulate ingredients of preheating, defect dynamics and false-vacuum decay. It is an analogue quantum simulator, however: the condensate implements the sine-Gordon universality class over a finite momentum and parameter range, not the Standard Model or an actual cosmological spacetime. Quantitative conclusions about cosmology require a controlled mapping of scales, initial states and observables.

#### Cluster-based sampling outperforms active learning across a large materials benchmark

Quinn Gallagher, Sonia Hasko and Michael Webb compared **100 space-filling and active-learning algorithms across 60 chemical and materials property-prediction tasks** in a **peer-reviewed Nature Computational Science analysis published 18 November**. When training examples had to be chosen from a fixed candidate library, cluster-based selection consistently performed best across representation dimensionality, fixed and learned representations, and training-set size. A Gaussian-process-variance argument identifies cluster-based selection as optimal in the low-data limit. [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-026-01076-9).

This challenges the common assumption that uncertainty-driven active learning is automatically the most data-efficient acquisition strategy. The benchmark concerns selection from an already defined library; adaptive experiments that can generate candidates outside that library may behave differently. Performance also remains dependent on dataset coverage, property smoothness and representation quality. **Evidence access:** the abstract, figure descriptions and data/code statement were reviewed; the subscription-only full methods and supplementary comparisons were inaccessible at the cutoff.

#### A human hypothalamus atlas maps selective vulnerability in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

Dan Yu and colleagues present **HypoAD** in an **open-access, peer-reviewed Nature article published 18 November**. The atlas combines high-resolution MRI from **458 people** with single-nucleus RNA sequencing of **614,403 nuclei** from young adults, people with Alzheimer’s disease and age-matched non-dementia controls. Subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian function showed particularly strong age- and Alzheimer-associated differences in volume and gene expression. [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11305-w).

The work links regional anatomy to cell-type-resolved transcription and supplies public sequencing and analysis resources. Cross-sectional tissue and imaging comparisons cannot determine whether the hypothalamic changes cause neurodegeneration, result from it or reflect comorbid ageing processes. Post-mortem sampling, cohort composition and the correspondence between donor tissue and living MRI cohorts also limit direct clinical inference. **Evidence access:** the full abstract, data statement and indexed article metadata were reviewed; detailed supplementary analyses were not accessible.

#### Amazon leaf shedding is widespread and often decoupled from canopy greenness

Guangqin Song and colleagues combined **10-m Sentinel-2 observations** with machine learning in an **open-access, peer-reviewed Nature article published 18 November**. Across **70.0% of the Amazon**, inferred leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least three months, contradicting the usual representation of the forest as uniformly evergreen. Hydroclimate was the dominant correlate of this asynchrony across **51.6%** of the basin, followed by soil properties (**33.2%**) and light availability (**15.2%**). [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11284-y).

Adding deciduousness-constrained turnover and leaf-age structure improved seasonal agreement between modelled gross primary productivity and satellite-derived photosynthetic seasonality across **79.9%** of the basin. These percentages describe spatial model attribution and agreement, not controlled causal effects. Cloud contamination, optical signals from multilayer canopies and sparse ground validation remain limitations; the result argues for revising carbon-cycle phenology models rather than supplying a direct new estimate of total Amazon carbon uptake.

#### Late Homo erectus occupied southern Chinese rainforest environments

Kira Westaway and colleagues report in an **open-access, peer-reviewed Nature article published 18 November** nine hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves in Guangxi, eight identified morphologically and genetically as **Homo erectus**. The team integrated **43 radiometric ages from five techniques** with two Bayesian age models, placing the occupation between **324 and 184 thousand years ago**. Faunal evidence, stable and clumped isotopes, trace elements and strontium mapping indicate closed-canopy rainforest conditions and possible movement beyond the local karst. [Research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11155-6).

The result supplies the youngest securely dated H. erectus occurrence yet reported from China and weakens the view that the species was restricted to open woodland or grassland mosaics. The behavioural inference is more tentative than the dating: mobility estimates rely on limited strontium measurements, cave assemblages can mix material, and the environmental proxies do not reveal subsistence technology or continuous occupation. The authors’ possible range of roughly **250 km** should therefore be read as a hypothesis from provenance modelling, not a directly tracked migration.

#### Kuiper-belt dust preserves evidence for an isotopically heavy primordial water reservoir

**Catch-up — newly highlighted by NASA on 18 November; peer-reviewed paper published online 11 November and in Science Advances on 13 November.** Lindsay Keller and colleagues analysed **12 hydrated interplanetary dust particles**, roughly **10–30 μm** across, collected in Earth’s stratosphere. Very high solar-energetic-particle track densities support an Edgeworth–Kuiper-belt origin. Electron microscopy and ion-probe measurements show water-altered minerals whose oxygen isotopes require ice enriched in **¹⁷O and ¹⁸O** relative to inner-solar-system reservoirs. [Research article](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13753991/); [NASA announcement](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/science-news/2026/11/18/nasa-scientists-find-clues-to-ancient-ice-beyond-neptune/).

The isotopic and mineralogical differences from CI chondrites and Bennu/Ryugu material support limited mixing between outer and inner formation regions, possibly because Saturn or the ice giants impeded inward drift. That barrier explanation is an inference from the samples and dynamical models. The particles’ provenance rests on exposure-track arguments, and twelve microscopic grains cannot measure the reservoir’s total mass or establish that all Kuiper-belt bodies shared the same water composition.

#### A plasma immunoassay measures a marker of advanced insoluble tau pathology

**Catch-up — peer-reviewed JAMA article published online 16 November and indexed in the 18 November research update.** Wagner Brum and colleagues tested a new plasma immunoassay for endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding-region tau in **728 participants**: 521 brain donors from two autopsy cohorts and 207 participants from two tau-PET cohorts in Canada and Sweden. Plasma eMTBR-tau rose with advanced neuropathological and PET Braak stage, identified regional tau-PET positivity and correlated strongly with mass-spectrometry eMTBR-tau243. [Research article](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2856953).

The assay could make measurement of a candidate blood marker for neocortical insoluble tau burden more scalable than mass spectrometry. This is a cross-sectional proof of principle, not a validated screening or diagnostic test: cohort-specific thresholds, longitudinal prediction, performance against clinical mimics and the effect of kidney or other systemic conditions still require prospective study. It should not be conflated with plasma p-tau217, which tracks amyloid-associated soluble tau biology more closely.
